title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: Agafea Mihalovna stepped out on tiptoe. The nurse let down the blind, chased a fly out from under the muslin canopy of the crib and a bumblebee that had been struggling against the window-frame, and sat down, fanning a faded birch branch over the mother and the baby.
"How hot it is. If only God would send a bit of rain," she said.

"Yes, yes, sh — sh — sh —" was all Kitty answered, rocking gently and tenderly squeezing the plump little arm with its rolls of fat at the wrist that Mitya was still waving weakly as he opened and closed his eyes. That hand kept tugging at Kitty; she longed to kiss it but was afraid she would wake him. Finally the little hand stopped waving and the eyes closed. From time to time, as he kept sucking, the baby raised his long, curly eyelashes and peeked at his mother with wet eyes that looked black in the twilight. The nurse had stopped fanning and was dozing off. From upstairs came the booming of the old prince's voice and Katavasov's chuckle.

"They've started talking without me," Kitty thought. "It is annoying that Kostya is out, though. He's probably back at the bee-house again. It's a pity he's there so often, but I'm glad of it. It takes his mind off things. He's so much happier and steadier now than he was in the spring. Back then he was so gloomy and tense I was frightened for him. And how funny he is!" she whispered, smiling.

She knew what was bothering her husband. It was his lack of faith. Even though, if anyone had asked her whether she believed that in the next life an unbeliever would be damned, she would have had to admit he would be, his unbelief did not make her unhappy. And while she accepted that for an unbeliever there could be no salvation, and loved her husband's soul more than anything in the world, she could still smile at his unbelief and tell herself he was simply absurd.

"What's the point of him reading philosophy of some kind all year long?" she wondered. "If everything's in those books, then he can understand them. If it's all wrong, why does he read them? He says himself that he would like to believe. So why doesn't he? Surely from thinking so much about it. And he thinks so much because he's so alone. He's always by himself. He can't talk about any of this with us. I think he'll be glad to have these visitors — especially Katavasov. He enjoys debates with them," she thought, and her mind jumped at once to the question of where it would be best to put Katavasov: in a room by himself, or sharing Sergey Ivanovitch's. Then an idea suddenly hit her that made her flinch hard enough to disturb Mitya, who shot her a stern look. "I'm sure the laundress hasn't sent the washing back yet, and all the best sheets are out. If I don't see to it, Agafea Mihalovna will give Sergey Ivanovitch the wrong sheets." At the very thought, the blood rushed into Kitty's face.

"Yes — I'll arrange it," she decided, and going back to her earlier train of thought, she remembered that some important spiritual question had been broken off, and she tried to recover what it was. "Yes — Kostya, the unbeliever," she thought again, smiling.
"All right, an unbeliever then! Better that than to be like Madame Stahl, or like what I tried to be back in those days abroad. No — he'll never put on an act about anything."

And a recent example of his goodness came vividly to mind. Two weeks earlier, a remorseful letter had arrived from Stepan Arkadyevitch to Dolly. He begged her to save his honor — to sell her estate to cover his debts. Dolly was in despair. She loathed her husband, despised him, pitied him, decided on a separation, decided to refuse, but in the end agreed to sell part of her property. After that — with a tender smile she couldn't hold back — Kitty remembered her husband's embarrassed awkwardness, his repeated clumsy attempts to bring up the subject, and how at last, having thought of the one way to help Dolly without bruising her pride, he had suggested to Kitty something that hadn't occurred to her before: that she should give up her own share of the property.

"He, an unbeliever — really! With that heart of his, that fear of hurting anyone, even a child! Everything for others, nothing for himself. Sergey Ivanovitch just takes it as Kostya's job to act as his steward. It's the same with his sister. Now Dolly and her children are under his protection — and all those peasants who come to him every day, as if he were obliged to be at their service."
"Yes — only be like your father, just like him," she said, handing Mitya back to the nurse and pressing her lips to his cheek.
